tldr: Tool-Planner is a task-planning framework that groups tools with similar or identical functionalities into toolkits using SimCSE-based clustering, enabling LLMs to reselect alternative tools within the same toolkit upon errors before resorting to cross-toolkit replanning, thereby improving planning efficiency and success rates.
contributions: Proposed Tool-Planner, a novel framework for task planning and tool invocation based on toolkits rather than individual tools
Tool clustering method using SimCSE embeddings and k-means++ to group APIs with similar/identical functionalities into toolkits
A two-level planning exploration strategy: first trying alternative APIs within the same toolkit, then replanning across toolkits only if all fail
Extensive experiments on ToolBench and APIBench showing state-of-the-art performance on 5 of 6 datasets
methods: The authors first extract tool documentation and descriptions from APIs, use LLMs to generate brief functionality explanations, and compute tool embeddings via SimCSE. These embeddings are clustered using k-means++ (k=1800 for ToolBench, k=65 for APIBench) into toolkits representing groups of similar tools. For planning, LLMs receive toolkit functionality descriptions via in-context learning to generate chained toolkit-based plans. When a tool error occurs, the framework prioritizes selecting an alternative API within the same toolkit without changing the plan; only if all APIs in a toolkit fail does it trigger cross-toolkit replanning at the toolkit level rather than the API level.
results: On ToolBench with GPT-4, Tool-Planner achieves +8.8% pass rate and +9.1% win rate compared to DFSDT (best baseline). On APIBench with GPT-4, it achieves +6.6% pass rate, +14.5% win rate, and -2.1% hallucination rate. For multi-tool instruction tasks (G2 and G3), pass rate increases by +8.9% and win rate by +10.6% on GPT-4. Tool-Planner achieves state-of-the-art performance on 5 out of 6 ToolBench datasets.
limitations: The paper notes that the number of identical or similar APIs within a toolkit is limited, so if all APIs in a toolkit fail, cross-toolkit replanning is still required. Additionally, while not extensively discussed, the approach depends on the quality of SimCSE embeddings and k-means++ clustering to produce meaningful tool groupings. No explicit ablation is shown on how clustering quality affects downstream performance.
